claim: pgvector applies metadata filters AFTER the HNSW index returns its ef_search candidates (post-filtering), so a WHERE clause can leave far fewer rows than the LIMIT requested.
quote: Post-filtering misses some good green candidates that were ignored because some others where selected.

claim: In a test, filtering color='green' with the HNSW index returned only 11 rows instead of the expected 15, and exact search found 23 closer matches the index missed.
quote: the HNSW index returned only 11 rows instead of the expected 15 ... the exact nearest neighbor search identified 23 additional closer matches that the approximate index search completely missed

claim: On a partitioned table with ~40M rows per partition at 768 dims, HNSW index creation stalled at 29.2% after 19+ hours even with maintenance_work_mem=40GB and 11 parallel workers.
quote: hnsw graph no longer fits into maintenance_work_mem after 570905 tuples

claim: HNSW builds run 10-50x slower on the disk-based path when the graph exceeds maintenance_work_mem (default 64MB), and Postgres emits a notice when this happens.
quote: Indexes build significantly faster when the graph fits into maintenance_work_mem

claim: With the default hnsw.ef_search of 40, a filter matching only 10% of rows yields on average just 4 results, so LIMIT can silently return fewer rows than requested before iterative scans (added in 0.8.0).
quote: If a condition matches 10% of rows, with HNSW and the default hnsw.ef_search of 40, only 4 rows will match on average.

claim: pgvector's indexable vector type tops out at 2,000 dimensions (halfvec to 4,000, bit to 64,000), HNSW indexes do not reclaim space on row deletes causing bloat and recall drift, and native sharding of vector data across nodes is not supported.
quote: HNSW indexes do not reclaim space when rows are deleted ... Native sharding of vector data across nodes is not supported

claim: A 10M-row table at 1,536 dims can take hours to index on a single core with indexes reaching tens of GB, and at 100M rows the vectors alone exceed 600GB before indexing.
quote: A 10M-row table with 1,536-dimensional embeddings can take hours to index on a single core ... At 100M rows, vectors alone exceed 600GB before indexing

claim: Filtered vector search latency can range from 50ms (pre-filter) to 5 seconds (post-filter), HNSW builds on a few million vectors can consume 10+GB RAM, and forcing overfetch (LIMIT 100 to get 10) gives no correctness guarantee.
quote: HNSW index creation on a few million vectors can consume 10+ GB of RAM or more

claim: A widely-discussed Hacker News thread 'The Case Against PGVector' debates pgvector's production tradeoffs around filtered search, scaling beyond cache, and OLTP resource contention.

pgvector is appropriate when the dataset fits one Postgres instance with moderate filter selectivity, but vector workloads share CPU/memory/IO with OLTP traffic and a burst of vector queries can starve transactional queries of buffer cache and parallel workers.
quote: a burst of vector queries can starve transactional queries of buffer cache and parallel workers

claim: Keeping embeddings fresh in pgvector is an operational burden: in-place batch re-embedding leaves the index in a partially-stale state, and the dominant cost is coordinating backfill and observability into which documents changed, not the API calls.
quote: Stale embeddings are a real RAG quality problem - when the vector store lags behind the source database, your retrieval quality degrades.

claim: The pgvector/pgvector repository has roughly 21.7k GitHub stars and documents hnsw.max_scan_tuples defaulting to 20000 as the cap on iterative scan depth.
quote: Supported types are: vector - up to 2,000 dimensions
